units.title: Embedding geometry and contrastive logits
outcomes: Explain why cosine similarity keeps angles and discards norms, and when that helps retrieval.
Derive NT-Xent as softmax cross-entropy over the \(2N-1\) other views, with \(1/\tau\) logit scaling.
Predict the loss for degenerate batches, including the \(\log(2N-1)\) uniform case.
units.why: Contrastive objectives compare directions, not positions. If norms leak into the logits, the loss rewards loud embeddings instead of aligned ones.

next.note: Scale the logits you derived here with temperature and test batch-size effects.
Implement the log-sum-exp and reduction the denominator needs.

study.title: NT-Xent and cosine similarity
study.locator: Section 2.1, Eq. (1): \(\operatorname{sim}(u,v)\) as the L2-normalized dot product and \(l_{i,j}\) with the sum over \(k \ne i\); Algorithm 1 for the full loop

study.title: Why normalization matters
study.locator: Section 5.1, Table 5: L2 Yes versus No rows, with the sentence that normalization plus temperature weights examples by hardness
study.depth: Skip the temperature-value comparison; the next unit owns \(\tau\).

focus: Cosine similarity is a dot product after L2 normalization. Positive scaling of either vector changes nothing.
NT-Xent treats the \(2N-1\) other views as classes. The positive stays in the denominator, so the loss is a valid cross-entropy.
With identical embeddings every row is uniform at any \(\tau\), so the loss equals \(\log(2N-1)\): \(\log 3 = 1.0986\) for \(2N = 4\).
Without normalization, one large-norm embedding dominates every softmax row it appears in.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive \(l_{i,j}\) from softmax cross-entropy over pairwise similarities. Then compute the \(\tau = 1\) loss by hand for embeddings \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) and get 0.5514.
traps: Calling cosine similarity translation-invariant. It is invariant to positive scaling, not to shifts; centering the batch changes all angles.
Dropping the positive from the denominator. SimCLR sums over \(k \ne i\), which includes the positive; without it the loss can go negative.
Reading NT-Xent as fixed-class classification. The classes are the current batch views, so the same pair gets a different loss in different batches.

selfTest.q: Embeddings \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) at \(\tau = 1\) give loss 0.5514. Show the per-row terms.
selfTest.a: For row 0 the positive scores 1 and the two negatives score 0, so \(l = -1 + \log(e + 2) = 0.5514\). Rows 1, 2 and 3 match by symmetry, and the mean over all four rows is 0.5514.

selfTest.q: All four embeddings are identical. What is the loss at \(\tau = 1\)?
selfTest.a: \(\log 3 = 1.0986\). Every row is uniform over its three candidates, so each row contributes \(\log 3\).

selfTest.q: Why does SimCLR Table 5 favor L2 normalization?
selfTest.a: Raw dot products mix angle with norm, so loud vectors dominate the softmax. With normalization plus temperature the loss weights examples by relative hardness, and Top-1 rises from 57.2 to 64.4 at the best setting. Without normalization the contrastive accuracy is higher (91.7 versus 87.8) yet the representation is worse, so the pretext score does not measure representation quality.

selfTest.q: Is the positive pair part of its own denominator?
selfTest.a: Yes. The sum runs over all \(k \ne i\) including the positive index \(j\), which keeps the loss a proper cross-entropy bounded below by 0.

outcomes: Derive the \(1/\tau\) sharpening of logits and gradients, and predict saturation at small \(\tau\).
Explain how batch size sets the negative count and when longer training closes the gap.

study.locator: Section 5.1, Table 5: \(\tau\) 0.05, 0.1, 0.5 and 1.0 with L2 normalization; best Top-1 64.4 at \(\tau = 0.1\); the hard-negative weighting sentence

study.title: Batch size and training length
study.locator: Sections 2.2 and 5.2 with Figure 9: batch sizes 256 to 8192 with 16,382 negatives per positive at 8192; larger batches help early and the gap shrinks with longer training

study.title: Augmentation composition
study.locator: Section 3.1 with Figures 5 and 6: single transforms fail while crop plus color distortion wins; color histograms alone suffice as a shortcut

focus: Dividing by \(\tau\) multiplies every logit gap. Small \(\tau\) sharpens toward \(\operatorname{argmax}\); large \(\tau\) flattens toward uniform.
The positive-logit gradient is \(-(1 - p_{\text{pos}})/\tau\). Easy pairs saturate near zero gradient at small \(\tau\), so hard negatives drive learning.
Negatives per positive equal \(2(N-1)\): 510 at batch 256 and 16,382 at batch 8192. Longer training closes much of the batch gap.
Random crop plus color distortion wins because it blocks the color-histogram shortcut, not because either transform is strong alone.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the NT-Xent gradient for the positive similarity. For similarities \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), compute the \(\tau = 1\) softmax \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.665&0.245&0.090\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) with gradient -0.335, and the \(\tau = 0.1\) gradient of about -0.0005.
traps: Pushing \(\tau\) ever lower. Below 0.1 easy pairs saturate and a few hard negatives dominate; Table 5 drops from 64.4 at 0.1 to 59.7 at 0.05.
Assuming bigger batches always win. Figure 9 shows large gains at 100 epochs that mostly disappear with longer training on randomly resampled batches.

Letting labels choose positives and still calling the method self-supervised. SimCLR positives are two views of one image; once class labels pick positives, it is supervised contrastive learning and must be compared as such.

selfTest.q: Similarities \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) at \(\tau = 1\): what is the positive probability?
selfTest.a: \(e^2/(e^2 + e + 1) = 0.665\). The remaining mass splits 0.245 and 0.090.

selfTest.q: What happens to easy-pair gradients as \(\tau\) goes to 0?
selfTest.a: The softmax saturates to one-hot, so \((1 - p)/\tau\) goes to 0 for decided pairs and learning concentrates on the remaining hard pairs; too small stalls training.

selfTest.q: Batch 8192 gives how many negatives per positive, and why?
selfTest.a: 16,382. The batch holds \(2N = 16{,}384\) views; excluding the anchor and its positive leaves \(2N - 2\) negatives.

selfTest.q: Positive-identification accuracy is near perfect but linear evaluation is poor. What went wrong?
selfTest.a: The task is solvable by shortcut, such as color histograms under crop-only augmentation. Composition makes pairing harder and representations better.

study.title: Negative rule and augmentation shortcuts
study.locator: Section 2.1: all other \(2(N-1)\) views count as negatives, including same-class views; Section 3.1 with Figure 6: color histograms alone suffice to distinguish images

study.title: Collapse without stop-gradient
study.locator: Figure 2: 67.7 percent with stop-gradient versus 0.1 percent without, plus the per-channel spread plot; Table 1 row (a): no predictor also gives 0.1 percent

focus: An augmentation declares an invariance. Crop-only declares color histograms fair game, and the encoder takes that shortcut.
Every batch negative is repelled, including same-class images. At batch 8192 with 1000 balanced classes, each anchor repels about 16 same-class views.
Full collapse keeps per-dimension spread at zero and rank at one while the loss sits at \(\log(2N-1)\). Partial collapse needs the same checks, since its loss still falls.

SimSiam avoids collapse on positives alone with stop-gradient and a predictor. The constant solution still minimizes its loss; the paper shows that removing either piece collapses to 0.1 percent and offers an EM-style hypothesis, not a proof.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write the three-line collapse check (mean per-dimension std of the L2-normalized embeddings, mean norm, numerical rank with a stated tolerance) and run it on constant versus Gaussian 128-d embeddings: expect spread 0.0 versus about 0.088, which is \(1/\sqrt{128}\), and rank 1 versus 128.
traps: Trusting falling loss as proof of learning. Partial collapse keeps the loss falling while dimensions die; only spread and rank checks catch it.
Dismissing false negatives as rare. About 16 per anchor at SimCLR scale is a steady repulsive pressure on same-class views.
Crediting the predictor alone for SimSiam. Figure 2 shows stop-gradient removal by itself collapses to 0.1 percent.

selfTest.q: What does the middle plot of SimSiam Figure 2 show without stop-gradient?
selfTest.a: Per-channel std of the normalized output falls toward zero: the embeddings go constant and validation accuracy drops to 0.1 percent.

selfTest.q: Estimate same-class negatives per anchor at batch 8192 with 1000 balanced classes.
selfTest.a: About 16: 16,382 negatives divided by 1000 classes.

selfTest.q: Your embeddings have numerical rank 3 in a 128-d space, but the loss keeps falling. Is that collapse?
selfTest.a: Dimensional collapse: the loss can still fall inside the live subspace while most dimensions carry nothing. Report spread and the singular-value spectrum, and check the probe; a falling loss does not rule it out.

selfTest.q: Why does adding color distortion to cropping improve representations while making pairing harder?
selfTest.a: It removes the color-histogram shortcut, so the encoder must use shape and content that transfer.

study.title: Frozen linear probe on CIFAR
study.locator: Self_Supervised_Learning.ipynb: Classifier with frozen Model().f, Finetune a Linear Layer for Classification, Baseline Without Self-Supervised Learning versus With Self-Supervised Learning, Plot your Comparison

focus: Freeze the encoder (requires_grad False) and train only the head. Anything else measures supervised relearning.
Probe \(h\), the pre-projection features. In SimCLR Table 3, where rotation was added to the augmentations, the projector output \(z\) lost the rotation information that \(h\) kept.
Match budgets exactly: same data fraction, epochs and head settings for baseline and pretrained runs.
Split by source identity before augmenting. Two views of one image on opposite sides of the split leak the answer.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the frozen-probe loop: load the encoder, freeze all of \(f\), attach one linear layer, and train the head on the fixed 10 percent split. Then state what turns it into fine-tuning: unfreeze \(f\) and give its parameters to the optimizer, usually at a lower learning rate.
traps: Probing \(z\) instead of \(h\). In SimCLR Table 3 an MLP on \(h\) predicts rotation at 67.6 percent and one on \(z\) at 25.6, near the 25 percent chance level, because rotation was one of the augmentations.
Celebrating a probe win with mismatched budgets. A longer-trained or larger-split baseline can erase the gap.
Splitting augmented views independently. Near-duplicates across the split inflate retrieval and probe scores without teaching anything.

selfTest.q: Why does the notebook set requires_grad False on model.f?
selfTest.a: To freeze the encoder so test accuracy measures representation quality, following the SimCLR Section 2.3 protocol.

selfTest.q: Rotation prediction: \(h\) scores 67.6 percent, \(g(h)\) 25.6 percent. What does that tell you about probing?
selfTest.a: Probe \(h\). In that run rotation was one of the augmentations, so the contrastive loss trained \(z\) to ignore it; probing \(z\) understates what the encoder keeps.

selfTest.q: Your retrieval score rises after adding test pairs mined from the training distribution. Leak or gain?
selfTest.a: Suspect near-duplicate leakage first. Re-split by pair identity, re-run, and only then claim a gain.

selfTest.q: Your probe reaches a reference accuracy quoted in a notebook comment, but your baseline trained for fewer epochs. What can you claim?
selfTest.a: Nothing about the representation yet. Only a comparison with matched data fraction, epochs and head settings isolates the effect of pretraining.

study.title: Vision transformers and scale
study.locator: Sections 12.10.2-12.10.3 (pp. 229-232): \(16 \times 16\) patches with learned linear map and learned 1D positional encodings; Figure 12.17; SWin multi-scale windows in Figure 12.18

focus: Patchify is a disjoint row-major grid: \((H/p)\) by \((W/p)\) patches, each flattened to \(Cp^2\) values (768 for 3-channel 16px patches).
One convolution with kernel equal to stride equal to patch size does extraction plus projection; D2L output keeps one vector per patch.
Self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so order must be injected. D2L learns pos_embedding from random init; the UDL ViT learns 1D encodings too.
Halving patch size quadruples tokens, multiplies attention-score work by 16, and multiplies per-token projection and MLP work by 4.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, patchify a \(2 \times 2\) single-channel image with patch size 1 and show row-major order \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&1&2&3\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Then derive the (4, 36, 512) output shape from img_size 96 and patch 16.
traps: Using overlapping patches by default. ViT and D2L use stride equal to patch size, so patches are disjoint.
Equating the cls representation with patch averaging. The cls token is learned aggregation; D2L Exercise 2 asks you to implement averaging as an experiment, not an identity.
Assuming sinusoidal positions. Both D2L and the UDL ViT learn positional embeddings, so 2D layout must be learned from data.

selfTest.q: \(224 \times 224\) image, patch 16: patches and tokens?
selfTest.a: 196 patches, 197 tokens with cls.

selfTest.q: Why does a ViT need positional embeddings when a CNN needs none?
selfTest.a: Attention is permutation-equivariant (UDL Problem 12.3), so it cannot see order; convolution bakes locality and translation structure into the operation.

selfTest.q: Patch size 16 to 8 at fixed resolution: how does attention work scale?
selfTest.a: Tokens quadruple, so the attention matrix grows 16-fold.

selfTest.q: What does LazyConv2d with kernel 16 and stride 16 compute on the worked example?
selfTest.a: Patch extraction plus learned projection to 512-d, giving (4, 36, 512) for batch 4.

study.title: Projector heads and CLIP practice
study.locator: cs231n/simclr/model.py class Model: ResNet-50 backbone \(f\) giving the 2048-d feature \(h\), MLP head \(g\) giving \(z\), both returned L2-normalized; CLIP_DINO.ipynb: get_similarity_no_loop, clip_zero_shot_classifier, CLIPImageRetriever.retrieve

focus: The loss makes \(2N\) decisions per batch: each image picks its text and each text picks its image from \(N\) options.
Temperature is learned, not tuned: log-parameterized, started at 0.07, capped at 100x for stability.
Each pair trains against 32,767 in-batch negatives, so every step is a 32,768-way proxy classification.
Zero-shot builds the classifier from text at test time. Prompts are model inputs: the default template gains 1.3 percent and 80-prompt ensembling adds 3.5 percent on ImageNet.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the symmetric \(\tau = 1\) loss for similarity matrix \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]\): row losses 0.1269 and 0.3133 with mean 0.2201 in both directions.
traps: Assuming aligned embeddings understand new words. The text encoder embeds prompts; unseen vocabulary and slices degrade, so alignment quality stays slice-dependent.
Training one direction only. CLIP optimizes both image-to-text and text-to-image jointly over the same matrix.

Mixing up the two evaluation spaces. Zero-shot retrieval must use the shared projected space, because that is where images and texts are compared. For a linear probe, also test the features before the projection; SimCLR Section 4.2 found them better in its setup.

selfTest.q: Batch of \(N\) pairs: how many scores and how many decisions?
selfTest.a: \(N^2\) scores; \(2N\) decisions, \(N\) per direction.

selfTest.q: Why does CLIP learn \(\tau\), and with what guardrails?
selfTest.a: It sets the logit range for the softmax; learning avoids tuning it. Init 0.07, clipped at 100x scaling to prevent instability.

selfTest.q: What is a zero-shot classifier in CLIP terms?
selfTest.a: Cosine softmax with L2-normalized inputs, text-generated weights, no bias and temperature scaling; the text encoder generates the classifier.

selfTest.q: Prompt template plus ensembling: what gains on ImageNet?
selfTest.a: 1.3 percent from A photo of a {label}, another 3.5 percent from 80-prompt ensembling.

study.title: Graph encoding notebook
study.locator: Notebook 13.1, Graph Representation: adjacency and embedding encodings
study.depth: Open only if the \(A^L\) walk counting in Section 13.2 is unclear.

focus: \(A^L\) counts walks, not paths: revisits allowed. The diagonal of \(A^2\) holds node degrees.
Correct layers are permutation-equivariant: permuting node order permutes embeddings identically. Readouts for graph labels must be invariant.
Repeated averaging converges toward the random-walk stationary distribution, so deep stacks wash out local signal.
Two layers are the empirical norm: the original GCN and GraphSAGE both use two. Depth needs residual connections or similar fixes, not more of the same layer.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write one aggregate-then-update step for a single node. Then square the 3-node path adjacency and read off one length-2 walk from node 1 to node 3 and two from node 2 to itself.
traps: Counting paths with \(A^L\). Walks may revisit nodes; the book states this explicitly.
Expecting depth to help by default. Mean aggregation converges across nodes, so a 10-layer stack can underperform a 2-layer one.
Indexing nodes as an ordered input. If shuffling IDs changes predictions beyond permutation, the layer is wrong, not the data.

selfTest.q: Path 1-2-3: length-2 walks from 1 to 3, and from 2 to 2?
selfTest.a: One (1-2-3) and two (2-1-2, 2-3-2), matching the \(A^2\) entries 1 and 2.

selfTest.q: What must a permutation of node order do to layer outputs?
selfTest.a: Permute them identically (equivariance); a graph-level readout must stay unchanged (invariance).

selfTest.q: All node embeddings look identical after six layers. Diagnose and name the mechanism.
selfTest.a: Oversmoothing from repeated neighborhood averaging toward the stationary distribution. Confirm per-layer cross-node spread, then cut depth or add residuals.

selfTest.q: Why do the original GCN and GraphSAGE use two layers?

practice.locator: Problems 13.1, 13.3, 13.5 and 13.7 (pp. 266-267): adjacency matrices, walk counts, the responsible permutation matrix, and the equivariance proof for the simple layer.

units.stopWhen: You solve Problems 13.1, 13.3, 13.5 and 13.7 without notes, and on a small graph you can show cross-node spread shrinking with depth under repeated mean aggregation.

fit.note: UDL Sections 13.1-13.4 with the Notes oversmoothing section and Problems 13.1-13.7 cover message passing, equivariance and oversmoothing recognition; Notebook 13.1 backs the encoding.
